materials_sci.atomic_packing_factor.title: Atomic packing factor of a unit cell

variables.name: APF
variables.desc: atomic packing factor (fraction of cell volume occupied by atoms)

variables.name: a
variables.desc: lattice parameter (cube edge for cubic cells)

assumptions: APF = (atoms/cell) x (atomic volume) / (cell volume). For FCC r = a/(2 sqrt 2) giving APF = pi/(3 sqrt 2) = 0.7405; BCC r = a sqrt(3)/4 gives sqrt(3) pi/8 = 0.6802; simple cubic r = a/2 gives pi/6 = 0.5236.

materials_sci.crystal_density.title: Density from crystal structure
assumptions: rho = (atoms/cell x molar mass) / (Avogadro x cell volume). Example values give copper (FCC, a = 0.3615 nm) rho ≈ 8.94 g/cm^3.
method_references: Theoretical density, rho = n A / (N_A V_cell)

materials_sci.miller_indices.title: Miller indices from intercepts

variables.name: intercepts
variables.desc: [x, y, z] axis intercepts as fractions of the lattice parameters (0 = parallel to that axis)

assumptions: Indices are the smallest integers proportional to the reciprocal intercepts; negative intercepts give negative indices. Enter intercepts as exact decimals (0.5, 0.25, ...).

materials_sci.interplanar_spacing_cubic.title: Interplanar spacing of a cubic lattice
assumptions: Cubic lattices only; non-cubic spacing needs the full lattice geometry.
method_references: Cubic interplanar spacing, d = a/sqrt(h^2 + k^2 + l^2)

materials_sci.bragg_law.title: Bragg's law (X-ray diffraction)
assumptions: theta is the Bragg angle; a powder diffractometer reports 2θ, so halve it before use.
method_references: Bragg's law, n lambda = 2 d sin(theta)

materials_sci.diffusion_arrhenius.title: Diffusion coefficient (Arrhenius)
assumptions: R = 8.314462618 J/(mol·K) is built in; enter Q in J/mol.

materials_sci.fick_first_law.title: Fick's first law (steady-state diffusion flux)

variables.name: J
variables.desc: diffusion flux (positive from C1 to C2)

assumptions: Steady state (concentration gradient constant); the general vector form is J = -D dC/dx.

materials_sci.fick_second_law.title: Fick's second law (non-steady, semi-infinite solid)

variables.name: C
variables.desc: concentration at depth x and time t

assumptions: Constant surface concentration, semi-infinite solid: C = Cs - (Cs - C0) erf(x/(2 sqrt(D t))).

materials_sci.lever_rule.title: Lever rule (weight fractions of two phases)
assumptions: Two-phase region of a binary phase diagram; C_alpha and C_beta are read from the tie line at the temperature of interest. Compositions are dimensionless fractions (wt fraction or at fraction).

materials_sci.hall_petch.title: Hall-Petch yield strength vs grain size
assumptions: sigma_y = sigma0 + k/sqrt(d). Empirical; breaks down (inverse Hall-Petch) below ~10-20 nm, which is not modelled.

materials_sci.true_stress_strain.title: True stress and true strain from engineering values
assumptions: Valid up to necking (constant-volume plastic flow). Beyond necking the true stress needs a Bridgman correction for triaxiality.

materials_sci.strain_hardening.title: Strain-hardening exponent and strength coefficient (power law)
assumptions: Power-law true stress-strain curve sigma = K epsilon^n fitted between two points; 0 < n < 1 for most metals.
method_references: Hollomon power-law fit, sigma = K epsilon^n

materials_sci.ductility.title: Percent elongation and reduction of area

variables.name: EL
variables.desc: elongation (fraction of the original gauge length; ×100 = %)

assumptions: Reported as fractions here; multiply by 100 for the usual percentage. Elongation depends on gauge length for a necked specimen.
method_references: Percent elongation and reduction of area definitions

materials_sci.brinell_hardness.title: Brinell hardness from indentation

variables.name: HB
variables.desc: Brinell hardness as a pressure (the conventional HB number = HB/9.80665e6 kgf/mm^2)

assumptions: Standard Brinell definition with P in N and D, d in m; the conventional HB number is this pressure in kgf/mm^2 (divide by 9.80665e6).

materials_sci.hardness_uts.title: Approximate UTS from Brinell hardness (steels)
assumptions: UTS(MPa) ≈ 3.45 × HB for carbon and alloy steels (HB ≲ 400). Approximate only — use a real tensile test for design. Tabular ASTM E140 conversions are NOT provided (not recalled).
method_references: Rule of thumb UTS ≈ 3.45 HB MPa (approximate; recalled)

materials_sci.charpy_impact.title: Charpy impact toughness (energy per fracture area)

variables.name: A
variables.desc: cross-sectional area at the notch (or ligament area)

assumptions: Normalizes the measured impact energy by the fractured area; the value depends on notch geometry and test temperature (the ductile-brittle transition is empirical — see report).

materials_sci.creep_rate.title: Steady-state creep rate (Norton power law)

variables.name: A
variables.desc: creep constant in 1/(s·Pa^n) — its value must match the Pa you use for sigma

variables.name: sigma
variables.desc: applied stress (Pa; A must be consistent with this)
variables.label: σ

assumptions: Steady-state (secondary) creep only: edot = A sigma^n exp(-Q/RT) with R = 8.314462618 J/(mol·K). sigma is entered in Pa, so A must carry units of 1/(s·Pa^n) (its value depends on n and on the stress unit); enter a bare number with those units kept consistent.

materials_sci.larson_miller.title: Larson-Miller parameter and rupture time

variables.name: C
variables.desc: Larson-Miller material constant (≈ 20 for many alloys)

variables.name: t_r
variables.desc: time to rupture in hours (bare number of hours)

assumptions: LMP = T (C + log10 t) with T in kelvin and t_r the rupture time in hours; C is a material constant. Solve for t_r to get rupture time at a given LMP and T.

materials_sci.corrosion_rate.title: Corrosion (penetration) rate from mass loss
assumptions: Uniform corrosion: penetration rate = mass loss / (density x area x time). Convert to mm/yr by multiplying by 3.1536e7 s/yr x 1000 mm/m (or enter t in years).
method_references: Corrosion rate from mass loss (ASTM G1 form, unit-consistent)

materials_sci.galvanic_potential.title: Galvanic couple potential difference
assumptions: Potentials are standard electrode potentials (vs SHE) or galvanic-series potentials from a table — user inputs, not built in. A larger positive E_cell means a stronger driving force.
method_references: Galvanic cell potential, E = E_cathode - E_anode

materials_sci.composite_modulus.title: Composite rule-of-mixtures moduli (fibre/matrix)
assumptions: Longitudinal modulus is the isostrain (Voigt) rule of mixtures; transverse is the isostress (Reuss) bound (it underestimates the true transverse modulus).
method_references: Rule of mixtures for fibre composites

materials_sci.composite_strength.title: Composite longitudinal strength (rule of mixtures)

variables.name: sigma_m
variables.desc: matrix stress at fibre fracture strain

assumptions: Longitudinal (isostrain) strength. Transverse strength is matrix-limited and not a simple rule of mixtures, so it is not provided.

materials_sci.elastic_bounds.title: Isotropic two-phase elastic bounds (Voigt, Reuss, Hashin-Shtrikman)

variables.name: E_voigt
variables.desc: isotropic E from the Voigt (isostrain) K and G

variables.name: E_reuss
variables.desc: isotropic E from the Reuss (isostress) K and G

assumptions: Isotropic two-phase bounds on the effective bulk and shear moduli; E values are the isotropic E = 9KG/(3K+G) for each bound pair. Voigt/Reuss are isostrain/isostress; Hashin-Shtrikman is the tightest bound for well-ordered isotropic phases.

materials_sci.laminate_clt.title: Composite laminate stiffness (classical lamination theory)

procedure.python:
def _laminate(v):
    """Classical lamination theory: A, B, D matrices and in-plane constants from a ply list.

    plies: [[thickness (m), angle (deg)], ...] bottom-to-top, one material for all plies. Reduced
    stiffness Q from E1, E2, nu12, G12; transformed to global axes by the standard CLT transformation;
    A = sum Q_bar t, B = 1/2 sum Q_bar (z^2 - z0^2), D = 1/3 sum Q_bar (z^3 - z0^3). In-plane (membrane)
    constants come from the compliance a = A^-1: E_x = 1/(h a11), E_y = 1/(h a22), G_xy = 1/(h a66),
    nu_xy = -a12/a11. These are exact for symmetric laminates (B = 0); for unsymmetric layups they come
    from A alone and ignore bending-extension coupling.
    """
    plies = v['plies']
    E1, E2, nu12, G12 = v['E1'], v['E2'], v['nu12'], v['G12']
    if not isinstance(plies, list) or not plies:
        raise MechError('plies: [[thickness (m), angle (deg)], ...] bottom-to-top')
    nu21 = nu12 * E2 / E1
    denom = 1.0 - nu12 * nu21
    if denom <= 0:
        raise MechError('nu12*nu21 must be less than 1')
    Q11, Q22, Q12, Q66 = E1 / denom, E2 / denom, nu12 * E2 / denom, G12
    total = sum(float(row[0]) for row in plies)
    if total <= 0:
        raise MechError('plies: total thickness must be positive')
    A = np.zeros((3, 3))
    B = np.zeros((3, 3))
    D = np.zeros((3, 3))
    z = -total / 2.0  # z measured from the laminate mid-plane
    for row in plies:
        t = float(row[0])
        th = math.radians(float(row[1]))
        zt = z + t
        m, n = math.cos(th), math.sin(th)
        m2, n2 = m * m, n * n
        Qb = np.zeros((3, 3))
        Qb[0, 0] = Q11 * m ** 4 + 2 * (Q12 + 2 * Q66) * m2 * n2 + Q22 * n ** 4
        Qb[0, 1] = (Q11 + Q22 - 4 * Q66) * m2 * n2 + Q12 * (m ** 4 + n ** 4)
        Qb[1, 1] = Q11 * n ** 4 + 2 * (Q12 + 2 * Q66) * m2 * n2 + Q22 * m ** 4
        Qb[0, 2] = (Q11 - Q12 - 2 * Q66) * m ** 3 * n + (Q12 - Q22 + 2 * Q66) * m * n ** 3
        Qb[1, 2] = (Q11 - Q12 - 2 * Q66) * m * n ** 3 + (Q12 - Q22 + 2 * Q66) * m ** 3 * n
        Qb[2, 2] = (Q11 + Q22 - 2 * Q12 - 2 * Q66) * m2 * n2 + Q66 * (m ** 4 + n ** 4)
        Qb[1, 0], Qb[2, 0], Qb[2, 1] = Qb[0, 1], Qb[0, 2], Qb[1, 2]
        A += Qb * (zt - z)
        B += Qb * (zt ** 2 - z ** 2) / 2.0
        D += Qb * (zt ** 3 - z ** 3) / 3.0
        z = zt
    h = total
    if h <= 0:
        raise MechError('plies: total thickness must be positive')
    if A[1, 1] <= 0 or A[0, 0] <= 0:
        raise MechError('A matrix is singular (check E1, E2 and ply angles)')
    a = np.linalg.inv(A)
    return {'E_x': 1.0 / (h * a[0, 0]), 'E_y': 1.0 / (h * a[1, 1]), 'nu_xy': -a[0, 1] / a[0, 0],
            'G_xy': 1.0 / (h * a[2, 2]), 'h': h, 'A': A.tolist(), 'B': B.tolist(), 'D': D.tolist()}

assumptions: One material for all plies; Q transformed to global axes by the standard CLT transformation. A = sum(Q_bar t), B = 1/2 sum(Q_bar (z2^2 - z1^2)), D = 1/3 sum(Q_bar (z2^3 - z1^3)). The membrane constants come from the compliance a = A^-1 (E_x = 1/(h a11), E_y = 1/(h a22), G_xy = 1/(h a66), nu_xy = -a12/a11) and are exact for symmetric laminates (B = 0); for unsymmetric laminates bending-extension coupling makes the true laminate moduli differ.
method_references: Classical lamination theory (Jones, Mechanics of Composite Materials; recalled)

cases.classification: reference landmark; original citation confidence retained in source; not a certified external benchmark

source.ref: BCC landmark: APF = sqrt(3) pi/8 = 0.68017 (universal textbook result; recalled). Input r = a sqrt(3)/4 for BCC.

source.derivation: C_0 = C_beta - W_alpha(C_beta - C_alpha) = 0.9 - 0.6875 x 0.8 = 0.9 - 0.55 = 0.35; W_beta = 1 - W_alpha = 0.3125
sigma_true = sigma_eng(1 + eps) = 300 x 1.1 = 330 MPa; eps_true = ln(1.1) = 0.095310
UTS = 3.45 MPa x HB = 3.45 x 200 = 690 MPa (approximate, steels)
sigma_L = V_f sigma_f + V_m sigma_m = 0.4 x 3.5e9 + 0.6 x 30e6 = 1.4e9 + 1.8e7 = 1.418e9 Pa

Single off-axis ply (30 deg) has shear-extension coupling A16, A26 != 0, so the membrane constants need the full compliance a = A^-1 (E_x = 1/(h a11), G_xy = 1/(h a66), nu_xy = -a12/a11). Reference computed with a numpy 3x3 inverse of A = Qbar(30 deg) x 1 mm (independent of mechcalc): E_x = 20.725 GPa, E_y = 10.724 GPa, G_xy = 7.2993 GPa, nu_xy = 0.38860.

Symmetric [0/45/0] layup (3 plies x 1 mm): A = Qbar(0) t + Qbar(45) t + Qbar(0) t, B = 0 by symmetry. Membrane constants from a = A^-1 (numpy 3x3 inverse, independent of mechcalc): E_x = 71.805 GPa, E_y = 13.017 GPa, G_xy = 8.7688 GPa, nu_xy = 0.40011.
